  "candidates": [
    {
      "startEvent":145,
      "endEvent":146,
      "contextStartEvent":113,
      "contextEndEvent":193,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"if God's existence is even possible then God must exist",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The compact conclusion summarizes the modal argument developed at E113–170. E174–192 explicitly locates the dispute in the possibility premise and offers apparent coherence as its support. Contesting that premise does not make the summary a replacement for reasoning.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Craig identifies conceptual incoherence as a relevant objection at E179–188 and answers the pizza objection at E1539–1552. He does not declare objections inadmissible regardless of their merits.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A compressed statement of a conditional philosophical argument whose controversial first premise remains open to challenge."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":303,
      "endEvent":305,
      "contextStartEvent":295,
      "contextEndEvent":383,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"if God does not exist objective moral values do not exist",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E306–362 supplies an evolutionary account and argues that adaptive or socially approved behavior does not thereby acquire belief-independent moral authority. E363–381 supplies a separate appeal to moral experience. These reasons are disputable but actually given.",
      "protectionExplanation":"No critic is excluded for rejecting the premise. E1667–1708 and E2309–2325 further explain the intended distinction between moral foundations and learning moral values.",
      "emotionalDevices":["shame"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A stated premise in an argument, illustrated with morally disturbing examples, rather than an unsupported loyalty test."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":448,
      "endEvent":450,
      "contextStartEvent":384,
      "contextEndEvent":454,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"the simple fact is that there just is no plausible naturalistic explanation of these facts",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"yes",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E407–438 provides the three phenomena to explain. E443–447 names two alternatives and says scholarship rejects them, but supplies no reasons for those rejections. The affirmation performs the additional work of eliminating natural explanations, which the cited facts alone do not accomplish. Later discussion chiefly supports historicity and scholarly agreement, not this exhaustive explanatory exclusion.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The wording is sweeping, but it does not expressly make alternative explanations impossible to consider. Craig engages historical objections later, including E2004–2050 and E2484–2507.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A time-limited summary of an asserted scholarly assessment; that assessment is reported rather than demonstrated within this exchange."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":464,
      "endEvent":466,
      "contextStartEvent":460,
      "contextEndEvent":489,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments simply by personally experiencing him",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E461–466 explicitly distinguishes experiential knowledge from a public argument. E467–475 explains the proposed analogy with directly experienced reality. It would misread this passage to treat the absence of an inference as an omitted public proof.",
      "protectionExplanation":"E476–479 asks listeners not to overlook inner experience, but does not instruct them to reject contrary evidence. E2053–2056 expressly allows good reasons for psychological misinterpretation to defeat the belief.",
      "emotionalDevices":["comfort"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A proposal that experience can provide defeasible personal warrant, alongside the separately offered public arguments."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":565,
      "endEvent":567,
      "contextStartEvent":553,
      "contextEndEvent":642,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"this absence of evidence is evidence of absence because it is evidence that should be there",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E568–583 explains the expected observable activity of the specified God. E584–605 supplies a proposed revelation test and claimed failures. The refrain at E606–608 concludes that application rather than supplying its entire rationale.",
      "protectionExplanation":"E635–640 explicitly says observations could have turned out otherwise and could support belief. The expectation that evidence should exist is disputable, but contrary findings are not excluded.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A memorable statement of an argument from missing expected evidence, illustrated partly through mocking descriptions of scriptural claims."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":632,
      "endEvent":634,
      "contextStartEvent":609,
      "contextEndEvent":642,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the absence of evidence for the efficacy of prayer is evidence for the absence of God",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E610–615 acknowledges that not every prayer must succeed and argues that some detectable benefit should emerge over many cases. E616–630 reports institutional studies and their negative findings. The conclusion summarizes those reasons, although the scope of the inference remains contestable.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Positive reports are described as failing scrutiny at E616–619, without enough detail to audit that assessment. Nevertheless, E635–640 expressly admits possible positive evidence; the text does not establish indiscriminate rejection of favorable results.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An empirical expectation argument, with the methodological details of the reported studies left unstated."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":676,
      "endEvent":678,
      "contextStartEvent":651,
      "contextEndEvent":678,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the absence of evidence through design in nature is evidence the absence of God",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E654–668 describes natural mechanisms for complexity; E669–675 adds the claim that imperfections fit unguided evolution better than intelligent design. The refrain summarizes an explanatory comparison rather than standing alone.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Stenger specifies features he regards as inconsistent with design. He does not say that every conceivable biological arrangement would favor his conclusion.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A concise conclusion from asserted comparative expectations about designed and evolved life."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":704,
      "endEvent":707,
      "contextStartEvent":680,
      "contextEndEvent":768,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the absence of evidence for creation of the universe is evidence the absence of God",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E680–704 gives energy and expansion considerations; E707–724 develops an expected-design comparison. E741–768 subsequently explains the narrower role of possible natural scenarios. The broad inference is contestable, but supported reasoning is supplied within the turn.",
      "protectionExplanation":"E715–724 expressly leaves room for a nonintervening creator. E761–768 acknowledges that the particular origin scenario is unproved. Neither move makes every observation confirm the nonexistence of every God.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],
      "confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A claim against an interventionist creator, grounded in an asserted absence of distinctive creative traces, rather than a proof against all conceivable creators."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":776,
      "endEvent":779,
      "contextStartEvent":769,
      "contextEndEvent":880,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the laws of physics are human inventions they are the ingredients of mathematical models",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E781–785 immediately qualifies the phrase: the laws are not arbitrary and must agree with observation. E786–845 develops the account through symmetry and the construction of physical models.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Agreement with observations is an express constraint. E851–858 welcomes possible violations of the current model, making the account answerable to contrary results.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A philosophical account of scientific descriptions, not a claim that physical behavior can be invented at will."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":906,
      "endEvent":908,
      "contextStartEvent":861,
      "contextEndEvent":908,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the universe is like the snowlake it's frozen nothing",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E865–875 defines the speaker's unusual use of 'nothing' as unstructured chaos. E891–906 gives a symmetry-breaking and phase-transition analogy. The metaphor compresses that account; its memorability does not itself replace the account.",
      "protectionExplanation":"At E1410–1416 Stenger accepts replacing 'nothing' with 'a chaotic region' when the terminology is challenged. That is a qualification rather than immunity from criticism.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An illustrative metaphor for emergence of structure, using an explicitly nonstandard meaning of nothing."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":949,
      "endEvent":952,
      "contextStartEvent":939,
      "contextEndEvent":952,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the very fact that there are non-believers in the world proves that God does not exist",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E940–949 argues that a good God would make himself available to everyone rather than reserve knowledge for favored believers while condemning others. The emphatic conclusion rests on that stated moral premise.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The hypothetical hidden God is rejected for a specified conflict with goodness and condemnation, not by declaring every form of disagreement or evidence defective. Craig directly disputes this premise at E1021–1036.",
      "emotionalDevices":["fear","identity"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A moral argument from hiddenness against a particular conception of God; 'proves' overstates what the contested premise settles."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1022,
      "endEvent":1026,
      "contextStartEvent":985,
      "contextEndEvent":1063,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"God could provide such evidence selectively only to persons who he knew would respond to it",
      "form":"no",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"unclear",
      "supportExplanation":"Craig offers a possible counterexample to Stenger's premise that God would probably supply objective evidence. E1030–1036 states the proposed justification: evidence need not be given to someone who would reject it. This is expressly a possibility argument, not an asserted report about every unbeliever.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The counterfactual about a person's response could shield selective evidence from inspection, because no evidence of that counterfactual is supplied. However, Craig does not explicitly identify all actual nonbelievers as unwilling, and E1040–1058 also argues that public evidence exists. Unrestricted protection is therefore not established.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A limited challenge to an expected-evidence premise, with an unresolved risk of making hiddenness explainable through inaccessible intentions."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1077,
      "endEvent":1078,
      "contextStartEvent":1073,
      "contextEndEvent":1108,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"I think this is rejection is something of a bad joke",
      "form":"no",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The ridicule is immediately followed by the journey and financial-balance analogies at E1085–1095 and the distinction between net energy and its components at E1096–1108. Stenger later disputes Craig's characterization at E1403–1409. That potential mischaracterization is separate from slogan substitution.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Craig gives an identifiable reason for rejecting the inference rather than saying that its proponent's disagreement alone establishes incompetence.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A derisive introduction to a substantive objection about confusing a zero balance with an absence of things requiring explanation."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1267,
      "endEvent":1270,
      "contextStartEvent":1251,
      "contextEndEvent":1292,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"logic tells you nothing that you don't already know tells you nothing that's not already built into the premises",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E1271–1284 explains the intended point: deduction establishes consequences of premises and cannot alone establish those premises about reality. E2071–2076 and E2432–2437 later clarify that premise quality, rather than valid inference itself, is disputed.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The formulation is sweeping but does not exclude logical criticism. Stenger explicitly concedes valid reasoning at E2432–2433 while challenging a premise.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An overstated but subsequently clarified reminder that a valid deduction needs warranted premises."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1511,
      "endEvent":1514,
      "contextStartEvent":1488,
      "contextEndEvent":1520,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"it only survived because the Roman Empire found it useful",
      "form":"no",
      "substitution":"yes",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The earlier discussion concerns historical attestation and scholarly disagreement about the empty tomb. Those points do not establish this exclusive explanation for Christianity's survival. E1515–1519 alleges subsequent suppression of rivals, but does not support the stronger 'only' claim. The assertion supplies an otherwise unestablished historical alternative.",
      "protectionExplanation":"No contrary historical evidence is expressly barred. The problem is the unsupported exclusivity of the explanation, not an immunity rule.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],
      "confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A compressed political explanation of religious survival, offered without enough supporting history in this transcript."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1519,
      "endEvent":1520,
      "contextStartEvent":1510,
      "contextEndEvent":1520,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"they were the Taliban of the ages",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E1515–1519 supplies the asserted basis for the analogy: suppressing religions and destroying temples and art. The comparison does not independently disprove the resurrection, but locally it summarizes the conduct just alleged.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The insult does not establish a rule dismissing all Christian claims or contrary evidence regardless of merits.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule","shame"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A condemnatory historical analogy attached to specific alleged conduct, rather than an independent proof about God's existence."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1733,
      "endEvent":1735,
      "contextStartEvent":1709,
      "contextEndEvent":1742,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"I've debated those guys that Dr Stinger talks about and none of their arguments have been able to hold up",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"yes",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"Craig has provided reasons for historical attestation and asserted majority agreement at E1713–1732. However, his own verdict on other debates substitutes for presenting the reasons that defeat the named dissenters' arguments. E2004–2038 later supplies more support for particular historical claims, not a demonstration that every dissenting argument failed.",
      "protectionExplanation":"A blanket retrospective verdict is not yet an explicit rule that any future objection must fail. E2278–2297 subsequently offers a narrower, assessable claim about whether those interlocutors disputed his description of the majority view.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An abbreviated appeal to prior debates as evidence of familiarity, overstretched into an unsupported comprehensive dismissal."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1891,
      "endEvent":1895,
      "contextStartEvent":1860,
      "contextEndEvent":1899,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"the absence of evidence can be taken as the evidence of absence when the evidence should be there is missing",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"This renewed use follows intervening replies and explicitly invokes the earlier examples at E1895–1899. Revelation, prayer, design and cosmology were discussed at E584–768. The refrain is a recap of that argument, not its only support.",
      "protectionExplanation":"E1866–1871 reiterates a possible positive test involving otherwise unavailable knowledge. Nothing here makes a successful result count against God.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A closing restatement of a conditional evidential principle whose application remains disputed."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1932,
      "endEvent":1933,
      "contextStartEvent":1900,
      "contextEndEvent":1933,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"Dr cig calls all that reasonable I call it preposterous",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E1903–1931 identifies the alleged tensions behind the verdict: cosmic scale, a special relationship with humanity, the incarnation, delay before humanity and limited habitability. The judgment is rhetorical, but it follows a stated criticism rather than replacing every reason.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The speaker ridicules a view, but does not make disagreement itself disqualify the respondent or prohibit explanations of those tensions.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An incredulous conclusion to an argument about apparent mismatch between cosmic history and human-centered theology."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":1969,
      "endEvent":1971,
      "contextStartEvent":1965,
      "contextEndEvent":1973,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"if you believe it's possible that God exists then God does exist",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"This renewed affirmation refers back to the modal argument at E113–192 and the response to the pizza analogy at E1539–1560. Its phrasing risks sliding from believing something possible to its actual modal possibility, but that does not erase the earlier reasoning.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The conclusion remains tied to the possibility premise; no new rule immunizes that premise from criticism.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A rhetorically simplified recap of the previously stated argument, not a fresh proof based solely on audience belief."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":2041,
      "endEvent":2044,
      "contextStartEvent":2004,
      "contextEndEvent":2050,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"his objections to the resurrection are not historical they're philosophical he doesn't believe in miracles",
      "form":"no",
      "substitution":"unclear",
      "protection":"unclear",
      "supportExplanation":"E2023–2038 quotes the scholar as accepting burial and an apparently empty tomb, supporting a distinction between accepting historical data and accepting a miracle. However, the transcript does not supply the scholar's full argument to establish Craig's further attribution of his objection to atheism.",
      "protectionExplanation":"E2043–2044 risks disposing of objections by assigning a worldview cause, but E2045–2048 asks only for openness to the possibility of miracles. It does not explicitly say that an atheist's historical or probabilistic objections must be disregarded regardless of content.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],
      "confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An attempt to separate historical premises from philosophical objections to miracle explanations, with insufficient source material to verify the characterization fully."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":2052,
      "endEvent":2056,
      "contextStartEvent":2050,
      "contextEndEvent":2066,
      "speaker":"B",
      "quote":"unless I have some good reason to think that I'm psychologically diluted it seems to me I'm perfectly rational to believe in God",
      "form":"no",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E2052–2053 invokes experienced reality and a changed life as personal warrant, continuing the explicitly experiential proposal at E460–479. The claim concerns the rationality of his own belief, not a standalone demonstration binding every listener.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The quoted 'unless' positively allows defeating reasons. E2057–2060 arguably overstates Stenger's position as requiring universal psychological delusion, but does not make the experience immune to all criticism.",
      "emotionalDevices":["comfort","identity"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A defeasible personal justification, combined with a disputable characterization of what the opposing explanation entails."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":2186,
      "endEvent":2187,
      "contextStartEvent":2155,
      "contextEndEvent":2187,
      "speaker":"A",
      "quote":"it's you God not I who have everything to answer for",
      "form":"yes",
      "substitution":"no",
      "protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E2155–2159 expressly introduces an imagined judgment-day encounter. E2161–2185 gives the moral complaint about suffering and avoidable limitations. The final line is the conclusion of that hypothetical address, not independent public proof.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The scenario assumes Stenger might be wrong. It neither makes disconfirmation impossible nor declares that every possible world would count against divine goodness.",
      "emotionalDevices":["shame"],
      "confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A dramatic moral challenge to a powerful creator, supported by examples within an explicitly hypothetical speech."
